network.overall_strategy: The network uses two feeder modules to generate 10 target-reaching paths without privileging one origin story. Module A makes alpha-ketoglutarate from glyoxylate plus pyruvate by either Fe2+-driven hydrothermal chemistry or phosphate-mediated surface chemistry, then closes to glutamate by four alternative downstream modules: fresh FeS reductive amination, electroreduced FeS amination, H2/Ni-surface amination, or cyanide/DAP hydantoin hydrolysis. Module B solves the C4 precursor problem with 3-cyanopropanal, obtained either explicitly by cyanosulfidic photochemistry from cyanoacetylene or speculatively by HCN addition to acrolein, followed by Strecker-type aminonitrile formation and hydrolysis. Mechanistically short-lived species are collapsed where they are not network hubs, pyroglutamate is included as the dominant sink/reservoir, and all productive routes are implicitly racemic.

reactions.name: Fe2+-promoted formation of alpha-ketoglutarate from pyruvate and glyoxylate

conditions.other: near-neutral Fe2+-rich water-rock interface; hydroxyketoglutarate and oxopentenedioate are compressed into this node

reactions.mechanism: Fe2+-assisted aldol coupling of glyoxylate and pyruvate gives hydroxyketoglutarate-like adducts that dehydrate and reduce to alpha-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: Fe2+ in warm aqueous networks promotes aldol coupling of pyruvate and glyoxylate, followed by dehydration/reduction to alpha-ketoglutarate (Muchowska et al., 2019). This is one of the better supported abiotic sources of alpha-KG, but I keep amination separate because integrated one-pot closure to glutamate remains unresolved and depends on ongoing glyoxylate supply (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Phosphate-mediated metal-free formation of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: pH ~7; concentrated phosphate; maloyl/fumaroyl-formate-like intermediates are compressed into this node

reactions.mechanism: Orthophosphate catalyzes aldol condensation and glyoxylate-driven redox rearrangement through alpha-ketoacid analogues to alpha-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: Stubbs et al. (2020) showed a metal-free, phosphate-catalyzed alpha-ketoacid network giving about 5% alpha-ketoglutarate from pyruvate plus glyoxylate at 50 C. This makes a surface-compatible alpha-KG source, though the yield is modest and the network still presumes glyoxylate availability.

reactions.name: Fresh FeS reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: pH 8-9.5 near the NH4+/NH3 pKa; fresh precipitate required

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the keto group to form an imine or iminium that is reduced on a fresh FeS surface to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Fresh FeS is the most chemically justified sulfide surface for this step: Huber and Wachtershauser (2003), building on Hafenbradl et al. (1995), reported reductive amination of alpha-oxo acids including glutamate near the NH4+/NH3 pKa, whereas other fresh metal sulfides were largely inactive. Exact primary glutamate yields are not well pinned down, but this route directly addresses the poor intrinsic reactivity of alpha-KG noted by Mayer and Moran (2022).

reactions.name: Electroreduced FeS amination of alpha-ketoglutarate
reactions.mechanism: An alpha-keto imine forms from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia, then accepts electrons from a reduced FeS surface to yield glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Electrochemically reduced FeS, used as an alkaline-vent analogue, converted several alpha-keto acids to amino acids in >50% yield, with glutamate and alanine formed preferentially (Kitadai et al., 2019). This is among the strongest glutamate-specific mineral-interface results, but it depends on maintaining a reduced FeS surface by geoelectrochemical gradients.

reactions.name: H2-driven Ni-surface reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: pH ~8; H2-rich mineral interface; competing alpha-hydroxyglutarate is not separately tracked

reactions.mechanism: A Ni surface activates H2 and reduces the alpha-keto imine generated from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) showed that Ni/SiO2-Al2O3, Pd/C, and Ni-bearing meteorite surfaces reduce alpha-KG with H2 and NH3 at pH 8 and room temperature, whereas no-catalyst controls do not. I choose a Ni-bearing alloy surface over Pd for prebiotic plausibility. The caveats are a competing alpha-hydroxyglutarate channel and the fact that glutamate was not detected when the same study tried to generate it one-pot from upstream ketoacid-forming chemistry.

reactions.name: Cyanide/DAP hydantoin formation from alpha-ketoglutarate
reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the ketoacid and, with amidating assistance, the adduct cyclizes to a 5-substituted hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) obtained the glutamate hydantoin from alpha-KG in very high yield (~96%) using cyanide with diamidophosphate. This is the clearest experimentally supported bridge between alpha-ketoacid and cyanide amino-acid chemistry, but it relies on DAP and cyanide availability, both of which remain debated.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamate hydantoin to glutamate

conditions.other: warm aqueous hydrolysis; incomplete conversion is expected

reactions.mechanism: The hydantoin ring opens and hydrolyzes to release the alpha-amino dicarboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Warm aqueous hydrolysis of the hydantoin released glutamate in about 19%, with most hydantoin still remaining (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). I therefore treat this as a real but bottlenecked closure step, not a high-yield endpoint.

reactions.name: Cyanosulfidic photoredox generation of 3-cyanopropanal from cyanoacetylene

conditions.other: UV irradiation (~254 nm), HS-/H2S photoreductant, sequential additions; maleonitrile and succinonitrile are compressed away

reactions.mechanism: Cyanoacetylene and HCN furnish dinitrile precursors that undergo UV/H2S photoreduction, ending with selective reduction of one nitrile to the aldehyde 3-cyanopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly derived the glutamate/glutamine branch from cyanoacetylene via maleonitrile, succinonitrile, and then 3-cyanopropanal under UV/H2S chemistry; Cu photoredox can accelerate the photoreductions. I compress those substeps into one node because the decisive bottleneck is generation of the C4 semialdehyde/nitrile precursor. The route is well evidenced but sequential rather than one-pot, and local sulfide availability is a real geochemical constraint (Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: HCN conjugate addition to acrolein

conditions.other: post-discharge condensate or evaporitic pool; mild basicity favors conjugate addition

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide performs Michael-type 1,4-addition to acrolein, generating beta-cyanopropionaldehyde after protonation.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) proposed acrolein, observed in discharge chemistry, as a glutamate precursor through HCN addition to give beta-cyanopropionaldehyde; Parker et al. (2011) retained this logic. The conjugate-addition chemistry is reasonable, but a prebiotic experiment closing this step to glutamate has not been shown, so this edge is explicitly speculative.

reactions.name: Strecker-type conversion of 3-cyanopropanal to glutamate aminonitrile

conditions.other: near-neutral to mildly basic HCN/NH3-rich pool; cyanohydrin substep not separately tracked

reactions.mechanism: The aldehyde first forms a cyanohydrin; ammonia then furnishes the alpha-aminonitrile center, giving the dinitrile precursor.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) reported that 3-cyanopropanal forms a cyanohydrin and then aminonitrile 54 upon addition of HCN and NH3. This is the only explicit de novo route in the provided literature to the immediate glutamate/glutamine aminonitrile precursor, though it requires staged reagent delivery and cyanide-rich conditions.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamate aminonitrile to glutamate

conditions.other: prolonged hydrolysis during wet-dry or geothermal cycling; full hydrolysis of both nitriles is needed for glutamate

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis convert both nitriles into carboxylates, yielding glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of aminonitriles to amino acids is the classical Strecker closure, and glutamate observed after hydrolysis of discharge residues is consistent with hidden nitrile precursors (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011). Patel et al. (2015) identify 54 as the precursor to glutamine and glutamate. However, mild prebiotic double-nitrile hydrolysis to glutamate has not been cleanly demonstrated for this exact substrate, so this edge is partly speculative and likely slow.

reactions.name: Cyclization of glutamate to pyroglutamate

conditions.other: acidic concentration or wet-dry heating; faster at low pH and above ~60 C

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular lactamization between the alpha-amino group and the gamma-carboxyl function gives a five-membered lactam with loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: Glutamate is unusually prone to cyclize to pyroglutamate during heating, concentration, and acidic exposure; hydrothermal flow experiments also show onward breakdown to succinate, formate, CO2, and NH3, partly suppressed by H2 (Lee et al., 2014). Solid-state and thermal studies likewise identify pyroglutamate as the dominant dehydration product (Wu et al., 2010; Weiss et al., 2018). I include this node because glutamate stability is a core constraint; reverse hydrolysis can occur, but forward cyclization dominates under drying and heating.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually coherent and supported in pieces by the literature, but not valid as written. rxn_001 is unbalanced and appears to omit an oxygen-containing coproduct or intermediate bookkeeping from the glyoxylate + pyruvate sequence. rxn_003 is more serious: direct alpha-ketoglutarate + NH3 -> glutamate is unbalanced, and as written the atom count would only close via an implausible O2 release; the fresh-FeS redox partner and water/byproducts are missing. The Hydrothermal -> Biochemical handoff is also not physically justified, and 'Biochemical' is not a prebiotic environment label.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_001 with explicit coproduct or intermediate accounting from the reported Fe2+-promoted sequence.
Rewrite rxn_003 to include the actual reducing equivalents and FeS oxidation bookkeeping, plus water/byproducts.
Replace 'Biochemical' with a defined FeS-rich prebiotic setting and specify pH and temperature.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-aligned hydrothermal branch because both modules map onto strong literature precedents and stay in a vent-like setting. It still fails conservation: rxn_001 is unbalanced, and rxn_004 omits the electrochemical/redox bookkeeping needed for electroreduced FeS amination; as written, direct alpha-ketoglutarate + NH3 -> glutamate leaves extra oxygen unaccounted for. The pathway idea is strong, but the network specification is not chemically valid until the reduced mineral state, electron source, and coproducts are explicit.
suggestions: Repair rxn_001 stoichiometry or expand it into the reported Fe2+-driven intermediate sequence.
Represent the reduced FeS or electrochemical input explicitly in rxn_004 instead of writing a direct net amination without redox bookkeeping.
Specify vent-relevant pH, NH4+/NH3 source, and electrochemical conditions for rxn_004.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The separate chemistry is plausible and literature-backed: Fe2+ chemistry can access alpha-ketoglutarate and Ni/H2 can aminate alpha-ketoglutarate. As written, rxn_001 remains unbalanced, and rxn_005 is also unbalanced and is most naturally corrected by adding H2O as product. The Ni/H2 step is mislabeled 'Biochemical'; the cited chemistry is mineral-catalyzed aqueous reduction and should also acknowledge the competing alpha-hydroxyglutarate channel reported under Ni/H2 conditions.
suggestions: Add the missing coproduct/intermediate accounting to rxn_001.
Add H2O as product in rxn_005 and specify the Ni catalyst, pH, and H2 pressure.
Replace 'Biochemical' with a defined H2-rich mineral surface environment and include the hydroxy-acid side branch.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This Bucherer-Bergs-type bridge is literature-aligned in spirit, but the node definitions are too compressed. rxn_006 is unbalanced and likely needs H2O as coproduct; it also cites DAP without including DAP as a reactant node. rxn_007 cannot be written as glutamate hydantoin -> glutamate alone; the balance check shows no single common small species fixes it, so hydrolysis water and carbon/nitrogen byproducts such as NH3 and CO2 must be explicit. The Hydrothermal -> Surface transfer is also left unexplained.
suggestions: Add DAP explicitly and repair rxn_006 with the missing coproduct, likely H2O.
Replace rxn_007 with a balanced hydrolysis sequence that includes water consumption and NH3/CO2 release.
Justify transport from the hydrothermal alpha-ketoglutarate setting to the surface hydantoin/hydrolysis setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The phosphate alpha-ketoglutarate module and fresh FeS amination each have literature precedent, but the pathway is weak as specified. rxn_002 is unbalanced and needs explicit coproduct or intermediate bookkeeping from the phosphate-mediated alpha-ketoacid network. rxn_003 is unbalanced and lacks the reducing/mineral stoichiometry for FeS amination, with the present formula bookkeeping effectively implying an implausible O2 release. The jump from a phosphate-rich surface setting to a 'Biochemical' environment is unsupported.
suggestions: Decompose rxn_002 into the reported phosphate-mediated intermediate sequence or add the omitted coproducts explicitly.
Rewrite rxn_003 with explicit redox partner, water/byproducts, and mineral-state bookkeeping.
Use a defined FeS-rich prebiotic environment instead of the 'Biochemical' label.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This branch combines two experimentally grounded modules, and the electroreduced FeS amination has strong literature support. However, rxn_002 remains unbalanced, and rxn_004 omits the redox bookkeeping required for electroreduced FeS chemistry. The surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is possible in principle but is not physically described, so environmental continuity is only moderate.
suggestions: Repair or expand rxn_002 so that the phosphate-mediated alpha-ketoglutarate sequence is mass-conserving.
Represent reduced FeS or explicit electrochemical input in rxn_004.
Justify how alpha-ketoglutarate formed in a phosphate-rich surface setting is transported into the vent-like FeS amination environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically this is one of the stronger two-step ideas: phosphate chemistry can give alpha-ketoglutarate, and Ni/H2 chemistry can aminate it. But the network still violates conservation: rxn_002 is unbalanced, and rxn_005 is missing H2O as product according to the balance check. The Ni/H2 step is again mislabeled 'Biochemical' rather than a defined mineral-catalyzed aqueous setting, and the literature warns that alpha-hydroxyglutarate competes strongly under Ni/H2 conditions.
suggestions: Repair or expand rxn_002 into a balanced phosphate-mediated alpha-ketoacid sequence.
Add H2O as product in rxn_005 and specify catalyst, pH, and H2 pressure.
Relabel the Ni/H2 step as a prebiotic mineral environment and include the competing hydroxy-acid branch.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Among the surface-only branches, this is the most environmentally coherent and it follows the literature bridge from alpha-ketoacids to hydantoins. The problems are stoichiometric and specification-level: rxn_002 is unbalanced, rxn_006 likely needs H2O as coproduct and should include DAP explicitly, and rxn_007 is not mass-conserving as written and should include hydrolysis water plus carbon/nitrogen byproducts. The pathway concept is sound, but the final closure to glutamate is not correctly encoded.
suggestions: Include DAP explicitly and repair rxn_006 with the missing coproduct, likely H2O.
Replace rxn_007 with a balanced hydrolysis sequence rather than a direct hydantoin -> glutamate edge.
Specify the temperature shift between hydantoin formation and hydrolysis so the surface setting is fully defined.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This captures the cyanosulfidic glutamate family only very approximately. rxn_008 is the main failure: the published chemistry is a multi-step UV/HS-/Cu sequence through maleonitrile and succinonitrile, whereas the network collapses it into an atom-nonconserving single step from cyanoacetylene + HCN + H2S to 3-cyanopropanal with no oxygen source. rxn_010 is close but missing H2O as product, and rxn_011 cannot be reduced to aminonitrile -> glutamate without explicit hydrolysis water and NH3 release. As written this pathway is not chemically valid.
suggestions: Split rxn_008 into the literature intermediates and include UV, HS-/H2S, Cu photoredox, and water as the oxygen source.
Add H2O as product to rxn_010.
Rewrite rxn_011 as a balanced nitrile-hydrolysis sequence with water consumption and NH3 byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The opening step is the network's only balanced reaction: rxn_009 is a chemically plausible HCN conjugate addition to acrolein. However, the literature treats this glutamate branch as speculative rather than experimentally closed. rxn_010 is unbalanced and likely needs H2O as product, while rxn_011 is severely underspecified because aminonitrile hydrolysis to glutamate must include water consumption and NH3 release. This pathway has a reasonable start but does not yet deliver a valid balanced route to glutamate.
suggestions: Keep rxn_009 as a low-confidence speculative branch unless supporting prebiotic yield data are supplied.
Add H2O as product to rxn_010.
Replace rxn_011 with a balanced multistep hydrolysis sequence that includes the missing water and nitrogen byproducts.

evaluation.network_feedback: Topology is adequate: 14 molecule nodes and 12 reaction nodes form a connected network with consistent IDs, and the dual-module strategy matches the two major glutamate families in the literature. The blocking issue is validity: the RDKit balance check flags 11 of 12 reactions as unbalanced, so the network is not mass-conserving as written; only rxn_009 is balanced. rxn_001 and rxn_002 need explicit coproduct or intermediate bookkeeping from the alpha-ketoglutarate-forming sequences, rxn_003 and rxn_004 need explicit reductant/electron bookkeeping rather than direct alpha-ketoglutarate + NH3 -> glutamate, rxn_005, rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_012 likely need H2O products, rxn_007 and rxn_011 cannot be repaired by a single small species and should include hydrolysis water plus NH3/CO2-type byproducts, and rxn_008 should be split into the Patel maleonitrile -> succinonitrile -> 3-cyanopropanal sequence with UV/HS-/Cu and an explicit oxygen source. Environmental consistency is mixed because 'Biochemical' is not a physical prebiotic environment, the cyanosulfidic branch lacks UV/Cu/sequential-delivery detail, and transfers between hydrothermal and surface modules are not justified. Literature alignment is otherwise good: the network explicitly includes both alpha-KG and nitrile families, treats the acrolein branch as speculative, and includes pyroglutamate as a sink/reservoir, but it does not solve the literature-highlighted one-pot coupling problem and rxn_012 should also release H2O if retained. Overall, this is a strategically well-informed but currently nonviable network specification, and no pathway reaches approval.
